t: #3447 Assign Elements to Groups with Constraints — Sieve of Smallest Indices
o: Each group of size g wants the earliest-indexed element that divides g. With both arrays up to 1e5, testing every element against every group is 1e10 operations — too slow. Example 3 shows the flavor: element 2 (index 0) serves all even groups, element 1 (index 1) all odd ones. Two efficient views exist: push each element out to its multiples (sieve style), or pull, by scanning each group's divisors.
k: Only the first occurrence of each element value matters — later duplicates never win.
Sieve: for each distinct element value v with index j, mark unmarked multiples of v with j.
Pull: for each group g, the answer is the minimum first-index among divisors of g.

a.i: Process elements in index order; the first time a value v is seen, record j on every multiple of v that is still unmarked. Total work is Σ (maxG / v) ≈ maxG · H(maxG), harmonic — fast. Later duplicates of v are skipped entirely.
s: For each new value v, sweep its multiples and fill unanswered slots with the current index.
a.t: O(E log E + n) where E = max value — harmonic sum over multiples

a.i: Keep first[v] = first index of value v. For each group g, trial-divide up to √g and take the minimum first-index over all divisors. This avoids touching memory proportional to the value range and is great when groups are sparse.
s: Build first-occurrence map of element values.
For each group, enumerate divisor pairs d and g/d.
Answer with the smallest first index found, else -1.

w: Prefer the sieve when the value range is dense; prefer divisor enumeration when groups are few or huge. Classic pitfall: forgetting that an element may serve many groups, or failing to skip duplicate element values (harmless for correctness but wasteful). Follow-up: answer many queries online — precompute best[] once and answer in O(1).
